newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian natives hold sit-in at Chretien's office.
newsitem.headline: Canadian natives hold sit-in at Chretien's office.

text.p: Native Indian leaders held a sit-in at Prime Minister Jean Chretien's office block on Thursday, insisting on a meeting to press demands for better treatment of aboriginals.

The top native leader, Ovide Mercredi, emerged from the Langevin Block in full feathered headdress more than two hours later and said Chretien's chief of staff, Jean Pelletier, had agreed to give a response by Friday noon (1600 GMT).
Chretien was not in the building and rarely if ever uses that office, preferring a suite in the Parliament buildings across the street. No one was hurt and no damage was reported during the sit-in.

"We had assurances from Mr. Pelletier that the prime minister will send us a letter by tomorrow noon indicating what his position is about the request that we made from him," said Mercredi, flanked by other Indian chiefs.
"The request was that we wanted him to set up a meeting with all the chiefs across the country so that we can begin working together on how the Royal Commission will be implemented in this country."
That was a reference to a report by the Royal Commission on Aboriginal Affairs issued in November after five years of work.

The report, to which the government has yet to react, urged Ottawa to give the natives control of more land and resources, and warned that failure by Canada to work out a fair relationship with natives "may well lead to violence."
Mercredi warned: "If he doesn't have a meeting with us, we'll just escalate the demonstrations and protests that we started today."
A spokeswoman for Chretien confirmed that Pelletier would provide a letter by noon.
Mercredi's formal title is national chief of the Assembly of First Nations. He had earlier called for a national day of action for Thursday.

Canada's natives have a high rate of suicide and drug abuse. They represent less than three percent of the Canadian population but account for 14 percent of inmates in federal prisons. Many live in poverty, and native leaders are struggling to break a dependence on federal assistance.
